questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundations of Agentic Coding and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 model training process begins with the selection of a suitable base model to serve as the foundation for continued pretraining. The research team evaluated several open-source candidates, including GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and DeepSeek V3.2, using three specific internal benchmarks described in Appendix B. These evaluations measured factual knowledge via FreshBench (an adversarial question-answer benchmark), state tracking capabilities through a custom benchmark similar to LoCoDiff but built from the team's private monorepo (reporting average character-level distance), and codebase perplexity (negative log-likelihood) on the same private monorepo. While Kimi K2.5 achieved the highest score on FreshBench (83.2%) but performed worse than DeepSeek V3.2 on state tracking and perplexity metrics, the team selected Kimi K2.5 as the base model. This decision was driven by its general strong performance across the evaluations combined with additional considerations regarding its efficiency within their specific infrastructure. Kimi K2.5 is a 1.04T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 32B active parameters.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundations of Agentic Coding and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 is designed to specialize the base model on coding knowledge and capabilities before reinforcement learning. This stage is explicitly divided into three distinct phases. First, the training spends the bulk of its compute at a 32k token sequence length. Second, it undergoes a shorter long-context extension phase that increases the sequence length to 256k. Finally, the stage concludes with a short Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) phase focused on targeted coding tasks. During the final two phases (the long-context extension and the SFT phase), Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers are included and trained jointly with the rest of the model.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundations of Agentic Coding and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: To serve the Composer 2 model faster in production, additional Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers are trained to enable speculative decoding. These MTP layers are initialized from scratch and trained on the same data mix as the main model, utilizing self-distillation to teach the layers to predict the exact logit distribution of the main language model head. To ensure this process generalizes effectively, the MTP layers are trained atop a checkpoint cut from the middle of the continued pretraining run. During the final two phases of training, which include long-context extension and SFT, the MTP layers are included and trained jointly with the rest of the model.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior Optimization
questions.lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL Training Regime and Policy Stability
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning pipeline operates in a highly asynchronous regime with independent training and rollout generation workers. To maintain stability in this environment, the system utilizes a single-epoch regime where the same prompt is never trained on twice. A critical strategy to minimize off-policy divergence involves fast weight synchronization and in-flight weight updates, allowing inference workers to update weights mid-rollout. Additionally, the system replays MoE routing to reduce divergence between the sampling and training policies. Unlike some prior works, the team opted not to mask rollouts that exceed the maximum sequence length, as benefits were not observed at small scale.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior Optimization
questions.lessonTitle: KL Divergence Estimator Selection for RL
questions.lessonContent: In the reinforcement learning process for Composer 2, Kullback–Leibler divergence is used for regularization, defined as KL(q ∥p) = Ex∼q[−log r(x)], where r(x) = p(x)/q(x). While the k3 estimator (defined as (r −1) −log r) is unbiased and reduces variance when policies p and q are close, its variance increases drastically as the policies diverge. The k2 estimator avoids this variance blow-up but is biased. Consequently, the training pipeline explicitly uses the standard estimator k1, defined as −log r, instead of k3. This choice ensures stable training by avoiding the extreme variance associated with large KL values found in the k3 estimator when policy distributions shift significantly.

correctness.explanation: The statement claims the Composer 2 training pipeline uses the k3 estimator for KL divergence. However, the source content explicitly states: 'Therefore, we use the standard estimator k1 = -log r instead' because the k3 estimator's variance increases drastically as p and q diverge. Thus, the statement is false.

grounding.explanation: The answer is a direct, self-contained, and accurate response to the true-false question. It is correctly grounded in the provided lesson content, which explicitly states that the k1 estimator is used instead of k3 to ensure stable training by avoiding the extreme variance associated with the k3 estimator.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior Optimization
questions.lessonTitle: Nonlinear Length Penalties for Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: To optimize agent behavior, Composer 2 applies a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty to the reward function. This penalty incentivizes the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests. The input for this penalty is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns. The nonlinearity ensures that on easy tasks, achievable with few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks. This approach enables the model to learn efficient behaviors, such as making multiple tool calls in parallel.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Real-World Evaluation, Infrastructure, and Performance Results
questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite designed to reflect the true distribution of real-world software engineering tasks by avoiding train-set contamination. Unlike public benchmarks that often feature highly specified prompts and isolated bug fixes, CursorBench tasks are derived from actual coding sessions within the engineering team. A key structural difference is the extent of code modification required; CursorBench tasks necessitate a median of 181 lines changed, whereas public benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual typically require only 7 to 10 lines. Additionally, the prompts in CursorBench are significantly more under-specified, with a median description length of just 390 characters compared to the 1,185 to 3,055 characters found in public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity accurately captures the complexity of real-world development.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Real-World Evaluation, Infrastructure, and Performance Results
questions.lessonContent: During the reinforcement learning of Composer 2, the model utilizes a Mixture-of-Experts architecture where numerical differences between the inference engine and the trainer can cause different experts to be selected for the same token. If the trainer and inference engine do not agree on expert routing, the log-probabilities computed during training may not match the distribution from which tokens were sampled, introducing noise into the policy gradient. To address this discrepancy, the system employs a technique called router replay. In this process, the inference engine returns the selected expert indices for every token at every MoE layer, and during the training forward pass, the router's expert assignment is overridden to match these returned indices. This ensures that the gradients flow correctly and maintains alignment between the sampling and training policies.

As the benchmark iterates, the complexity of the tasks grows significantly to prevent performance saturation. Specifically, tasks from CursorBench-3 involve changing more than twice as many files and lines of code on average compared to earlier versions of the benchmark.
